Listening part B, you hear an optometrist talking about amblyopia to parents and teachers at a kindergarten.
Now read the question.
I was asked here today to provide important information regarding amblyopia in children.
Oopia is a condition in which the nerve pathway from an affected eye to the brain is not properly
developed during childhood.
It is the most common visual impairment among children and affects up to 3% of the young
population.
However, because only one eye is usually affected and the other eye does the work at both, many
parents are unaware of the problem.
Fortunately, it can be easily detected with a thorough eye examination and the earlier
the condition is detected, the easier it is to treat.
Treatment depends on the particular cause of angiopia.
However, most commonly eyeglasses, prisms, and eye drops or patches are used to blow
the vision of the normal eye and force the brain to recognize the image from the eye
with angiopia.

Today, we are talking about side effects.
We'll look at the most common drugs first.
As you know, some patients suffer side effects and others don't, and not all patients suffer
the same side effects either. Let's consider ibuprofen, for example, a very
common pain medication. Some people may suffer dizziness and others might feel
nauseous. It's also possible to have diarrhea, vomiting, even headaches with
this type of pain medication. Injecting drugs intravenously may cause swelling
at the injection site for some patients. Stomach aches are a side effect of some
anti-allergy drugs as well as loss of appetite and constipation. Patients who take valium
may experience drowsiness while others may get a rash. Tremors are another side effect
of this drug.
Listening Part B. You hear a senior registrar talking about cholesterol to a group of junior
doctors. Now read the question.
The average total cholesterol level in the UK is 5.5 millimole per litre for men and
5.6 millimole per litre for women, which is above a normal level. So does that mean
that most people need to take anticholestral drugs? In recent years we've come to realise
that to decide whether an individual's cholesterol levels are dangerous, these levels need to
be considered in the light of the person's overall risk of heart disease. This overall
risk is determined by a combination of factors, including age, gender, family history of heart
disease and whether someone smokes is overweight, has high blood pressure or diabetes.
The higher the risk of heart disease, for example, a male smoker with high blood pressure
and diabetes, then the greater the need to get cholesterol levels down.
